blocks.text: Energy Inflation and the Two-Year Treasury
Investment memo | Data as of November 8, 2026 | Market prices as of November 6, 2026 | Generated from model run 2026-11-08T16:46:39

blocks.title: Recommendation: No trade at current prices
blocks.text: Buying the 2-year note (91282CRU7, 4.625% due October 31, 2028) instead of the 6-month bill does not offer an attractive edge at current prices.

runs: Held for 178 days from November 9, 2026 to May 6, 2027, the bill returns 2.08%. The note beats it only if the 1.5-year Treasury yield on May 6, 2027 is below 4.61%, which is the market's own forward rate. If the market has already priced EIA's gasoline forecast, the probability-weighted edge is -0.63% (-1.29% annualized). Even if the market prices flat gasoline, it is +0.00%.
Switch from the bill to the note if either of these happens:

items: The 2-year yield rises to 4.89% or higher (now 4.51%) with the gasoline outlook unchanged. At that price the expected edge reaches the 0.10% minimum even if EIA's forecast is priced in.

Retail gasoline averages at least 5% below EIA's path for a full month while the 2-year yield has not fallen. That is evidence for the below-EIA path, where the note beats the bill by +0.63% under the same view.

blocks.text: 2. Thesis: gasoline inflation is fading, but slowly in the data

runs: Pump prices are already falling. The October 2026 average retail price was $4.31, below EIA's $4.40 forecast for that month, and the latest weekly price is $4.15 (November 2, 2026). EIA's October 2026 outlook takes the monthly average to $3.66 by March 2027, a 15% decline.

Gasoline now weighs 4.08% of the CPI, so a 10% move in pump prices moves headline inflation by about 0.41 pp. Holding core at its trailing pace of 2.56%, food at 2.48% and other energy at 7.84% (assumptions), headline inflation reaches 2.7% by March 2027 if gasoline follows EIA, 3.2% if it holds at today's price and 3.7% if it rises as much as EIA expects it to fall. The latest reading is 3.7% for September 2026.

The decline shows up late. In the stable case, year-over-year inflation peaks at 4.1% in January 2027 and falls only in March 2027, largely because the March 2026 gasoline jump (+24.9% in one month) drops out of the comparison. That base effect is public, so the market sees it too. A data caveat pushes the same way: BLS never published October 2025 CPI, and core prices changed -0.11% from September to November 2025 against +0.26% over the same months a year earlier, a low base that lifts measured year-over-year inflation.

blocks.text: 3. What the market has priced in

runs: The forward rate is the market's price for the 1.5-year yield on May 6, 2027. Buying the note and financing it at the bill rate locks in 4.61%, so the note beats the bill exactly when the realized yield ends below that level: the breakeven and the forward are the same number. A cross-check from the whole par curve gives 4.61%.

Today's 2-year yield is 4.51%. If the curve did not move, the note would roll down to a 4.42% yield and beat the bill by 0.27%. The market instead prices the yield 19 bp higher: some expected tightening plus a term premium. The effective fed funds rate is 3.88%. The Federal Reserve Board's Kim-Wright model puts the 1-year and 2-year term premiums at 0.30% and 0.44% (October 30, 2026), so part of the forward is pay for bearing risk rather than an expected rate rise.

Scenario yields are assumptions: the forward plus or minus steps of 45 bp, half the interquartile range of 437 monthly forward errors since 1990. The two views differ only in which gasoline path the forward already contains: "market prices flat gasoline" puts today's price at the forward; "market prices EIA's forecast" puts EIA's path there.

blocks.note: Edge = note return minus bill return over the holding period, not annualized. Yields are 1.5-year yields at the horizon (assumptions). Below EIA has no probability.

runs: History offers a small edge that has nothing to do with gasoline. The realized yield has tended to end below the forward (median error -19 bp, mean -28 bp), which would be worth +0.27% to +0.40% over the bill for this hold. That comes from term premium and past easing cycles, and it reversed sharply in tightening years.

blocks.text: 4. Evidence: pass-through and the walk-forward test

runs: Module A regresses the monthly change in the CPI gasoline index (not seasonally adjusted) on the change in EIA's weekly retail price averaged by month, with two lags and calendar-month dummies, 1990-12 to 2026-09 (430 months). The same-month coefficient is 0.937 (standard error 0.011); the lags add 0.071 and -0.021, for total pass-through of 0.988 (not distinguishable from 1, p = 0.27). R² is 0.984 and the typical monthly miss is 0.74 pp.

The fit has known flaws. Misses reverse the next month (Durbin-Watson 2.65; Ljung-Box p = 0.000), probably because BLS and EIA price on different days. Miss size varies over time (Breusch-Pagan p = 0.034), so standard errors are robust to both. Big misses are more common than a normal curve predicts (kurtosis 5.6). The same-month coefficient drifts: 0.89, 0.98 and 0.94 across 1990-2007, 2008-2019 and 2020-2026.

Module B re-estimates the model on each of 308 CPI release dates from 2001-01 to 2026-09, using only data published by that morning (release dates checked against ALFRED vintages; a test scrambles all later data and confirms the forecasts do not change).

blocks.note: RMSE of the cumulative change in CPI gasoline. Ratio = model RMSE / benchmark RMSE; below 1 = model better. * = Diebold-Mariano p < 0.05.

runs: The model cuts the 1-month error by 74% against a no-change forecast, but only because it uses weekly prices already observed for the month in progress. By six months the gain is gone (ratio 0.96), and the seasonal benchmark wins from four months out. A simple rule, CPI gasoline moving one-for-one with retail prices, beat the estimated model at every horizon, so the scenarios use that rule and keep the estimated model as a sensitivity (headline paths differ by at most 0.04 pp). The largest 3-month misses came at oil turning points: Dec 2008 (-61 pp); Nov 2008 (-52 pp); Apr 2026 (+33 pp). Nothing here forecasts gasoline itself; the scenarios carry that risk.
Live check: with weekly prices through November 2, 2026, the 1:1 rule puts October 2026 CPI gasoline at -1.0% for the month (estimated model -0.4%).

blocks.text: 5. Scenario returns and expected return vs the bill

runs: The note's return falls about 0.35% for each 25 bp rise in the horizon yield (modified duration 1.87, convexity 4.47). It is priced at 100.214 clean (assumption: yield = Treasury's 2-year par yield, 4.51%).

With equal scenario probabilities, the expected edge is +0.00% if the market prices flat gasoline and -0.63% if it prices EIA's forecast. The trade needs gasoline below EIA's path ($3.22 by March 2027) or a cheaper entry point.

items: Core momentum: core inflation is running at 3.4% annualized over the last three months, against the 2.6% assumption; above 3.6% the stable and rising cases become more likely regardless of gasoline.
Oil supply: EIA's falling path depends on its oil outlook; if Brent runs $10 or more above EIA's path, the rising case is in play.
Policy reacts to core, not gasoline: a gasoline-only decline may not move the forward if core stays firm.
Data quality: the missing October 2025 CPI and low late-2025 base distort year-over-year comparisons.
Assumption risk: the scenario-to-yield mapping, step size and probabilities are judgment calls, and no futures data were available to anchor the gasoline path.

items: Only one inflation channel is modeled (retail gasoline to CPI gasoline); core, food and other energy are assumptions.
No federal funds rate forecast: rate paths are scenario assumptions anchored to Treasury forwards. SOFR and fed funds futures, and gasoline or Brent futures, were not available from free sources.
The note's price is derived from Treasury's par curve, not a dealer quote; bid-ask costs are ignored.
Relative-importance weights are rolled forward from December 2025; update them when BLS publishes the December 2026 table (www.bls.gov blocks scripted downloads, so this is a manual step).
Walk-forward results cover gasoline CPI only; the headline path has no out-of-sample test.
